topics.title: Life Processes
topics.description: How the body's organ systems keep us alive, and how nerves and hormones coordinate them.

lessons.title: Human Body Systems
objectives: Describe the main organ systems and their functions
Explain how the respiratory and circulatory systems work together
Explain the role of the kidneys in excretion and water balance
Explain homeostasis with examples
lessons.intro: Your body carries out thousands of activities every second without your noticing: breathing, digesting, pumping blood, filtering waste and keeping your temperature steady. These are life processes, and they are performed by organ systems, groups of organs working together. No system works alone. The respiratory, circulatory, digestive, excretory, nervous and endocrine systems cooperate to keep the internal environment stable, a condition called homeostasis.
sections: Nutrition, respiration and transport

The digestive system breaks food into small molecules such as glucose, amino acids and fatty acids, which are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine into the blood. The respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide: air passes through the nose, trachea and bronchi into millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli in the lungs, where oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. The circulatory system, made of the heart, blood vessels and blood, transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones and wastes. The human heart has four chambers, keeping oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood separate, which allows efficient oxygen supply. Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin.
Excretion

Cells produce wastes such as carbon dioxide and nitrogenous waste (urea). The excretory system removes them. Each kidney contains about a million filtering units called nephrons. Blood is filtered in the nephron; useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, salts and much of the water are reabsorbed, and the remaining waste forms urine, which passes through the ureters to the urinary bladder and out through the urethra. By adjusting how much water and salt are reabsorbed, the kidneys also regulate the body's water and ion balance. If the kidneys fail, a dialysis machine can filter the blood artificially.
Coordination and homeostasis

The nervous system detects changes and coordinates rapid responses using electrical signals, while the endocrine system uses hormones carried in the blood for slower, longer-lasting regulation. Homeostasis means maintaining stable internal conditions despite outside changes. During exercise, muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide, so breathing rate and heart rate both rise. When blood glucose rises after a meal, the pancreas releases insulin, which helps cells take up glucose; reduced insulin causes diabetes. When we are hot, we sweat to cool down. Damage to one system, such as a blocked artery, quickly affects others.
definitions: A group of organs working together to perform a function.
Tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange takes place.
The filtering unit of the kidney.
Maintenance of stable internal conditions in the body.
A chemical messenger secreted into the blood by an endocrine gland.
examples: During a race, breathing and heart rate increase to supply muscles with more oxygen.
Insulin injections help people with diabetes control their blood sugar.

worked.problem: Trace how oxygen from the air reaches a muscle cell in the leg.

Blood goes to the heart, which pumps it through arteries to the leg.
In capillaries of the muscle, oxygen diffuses into the muscle cells for respiration.
worked.answer: Lungs (alveoli) → blood (haemoglobin) → heart → arteries → capillaries → muscle cells.

lessons.real_world: Doctors measure blood pressure, blood sugar and kidney function to check how well these systems are working. Regular exercise strengthens the heart and lungs, and drinking enough water helps the kidneys maintain balance.
takeaways: Organ systems work together; none works alone.
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli; the four-chambered heart pumps blood efficiently.
Nephrons filter blood, reabsorb useful substances and form urine.
Nerves give fast responses; hormones give slower, longer ones; together they maintain homeostasis.

lessons.title: Control and Coordination
objectives: Describe the structure of a neuron and how impulses travel
Explain reflex actions and the reflex arc
Describe the main parts of the brain and their functions
Explain hormonal control in animals and plants
lessons.intro: Touch a hot pan and your hand jerks back before you even feel pain. See a ball coming and you raise your hands to catch it. Every movement and response in the body is controlled and coordinated so that organs work in harmony. Animals use two systems for this: the nervous system for fast responses and the endocrine (hormonal) system for slower, longer-lasting control. Plants, which have no nerves, coordinate using chemical substances.
sections: Neurons and reflexes

The nervous system is made of nerve cells called neurons. Information is picked up by receptors in sense organs and travels as electrical impulses: from the dendrites, through the cell body and along the axon. At the end of the axon, the impulse releases chemicals that cross a tiny gap, the synapse, to the next neuron. A reflex action is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus, such as withdrawing your hand from a flame or blinking when something approaches your eye. The pathway of a reflex, called a reflex arc, runs: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → effector (muscle). Because the spinal cord responds before the brain processes the signal, reflexes are very fast and protect us from harm.
The brain

The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. The forebrain, mainly the cerebrum, is the thinking part: it handles thinking, learning, memory, voluntary actions, and has regions for sight, hearing, smell and touch. The midbrain and hindbrain control involuntary actions. The medulla in the hindbrain controls blood pressure, breathing, salivation and vomiting. The cerebellum maintains posture and balance and makes voluntary movements precise, such as walking in a straight line or picking up a pencil. The brain is protected by the skull and a fluid-filled membrane, and the spinal cord by the vertebral column.
Hormones in animals and plants

Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the blood. The pituitary gland releases growth hormone, and too little causes dwarfism. The thyroid gland makes thyroxin, which needs iodine; iodine deficiency causes goitre, which is why iodised salt is used. Adrenaline from the adrenal glands prepares the body for emergencies, increasing heart rate and breathing. Insulin from the pancreas regulates blood sugar. Feedback mechanisms control hormone levels: when blood sugar rises, more insulin is released. Plants respond with plant hormones: auxin makes stems bend towards light (phototropism) by causing faster growth on the shaded side; gibberellins promote stem growth; cytokinins promote cell division; and abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes leaves to wilt.
definitions: A nerve cell that carries electrical impulses.
The gap between two neurons where signals pass chemically.
A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus.
A gland that secretes hormones directly into the blood.
Growth of a plant part in response to light.
examples: Sneezing and coughing are reflex actions that clear the airways.
A plant on a windowsill bends towards the light because of auxin.

worked.problem: Describe the reflex arc when you accidentally step on a sharp pin.
steps: Pain receptors in the skin of the foot detect the stimulus.
A sensory neuron carries the impulse to the spinal cord.
A relay neuron in the spinal cord passes it to a motor neuron.
The motor neuron carries the impulse to leg muscles (effector), which contract to lift the foot.
The message also reaches the brain, and you feel pain slightly later.
worked.answer: Receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → leg muscle; the foot lifts before the brain registers pain.

lessons.real_world: Doctors test the knee-jerk reflex to check the nervous system. Helmets protect the brain in accidents, iodised salt prevents goitre, and farmers use plant hormones to ripen fruit and increase crop growth.
takeaways: Neurons carry impulses; synapses pass them on chemically.
Reflex arcs pass through the spinal cord for rapid protective responses.
The cerebrum controls thinking; the cerebellum balance; the medulla involuntary actions.
Hormones such as insulin, thyroxin and adrenaline, and plant hormones such as auxin, regulate slower responses.

topics.title: Our Environment
topics.description: Ecosystems, food chains, energy flow and the sustainable management of natural resources.

lessons.title: Ecosystems
objectives: Describe the components of an ecosystem
Explain food chains, food webs and trophic levels
Explain energy flow and the 10 per cent law
Describe human impacts such as biological magnification and eutrophication
lessons.intro: A pond, a forest, a grassland and even a garden are ecosystems: communities of living organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings. Energy flows through an ecosystem from the Sun to plants and then to animals, while nutrients are recycled again and again. Understanding how ecosystems work explains why removing one species can affect many others and why pollution can travel up food chains.
sections: Components and food chains

An ecosystem has biotic components (plants, animals and microorganisms) and abiotic components (temperature, rainfall, soil, light and water). Producers, mainly green plants and algae, make food by photosynthesis. Consumers eat other organisms: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals and omnivores eat both. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. A food chain shows who eats whom: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle. Each step is a trophic level. In nature, organisms usually eat several kinds of food, so food chains interconnect to form food webs.
Energy flow

Energy enters an ecosystem when producers capture sunlight; they capture only about 1 per cent of the sunlight falling on leaves. At each trophic level, organisms use much of the energy for their own life processes, and much is lost as heat. On average, only about 10 per cent of the energy at one level is passed to the next; this is the 10 per cent law. So if plants contain 10,000 J, herbivores receive about 1,000 J and carnivores about 100 J. This is why food chains usually have only three or four levels and why there are fewer top predators than herbivores. Energy flow is unidirectional: it does not return to the Sun or to plants.
Human impact

Some harmful chemicals, such as pesticides, are not broken down and accumulate in organisms. Their concentration increases at each higher trophic level, a process called biological magnification, so top consumers, including humans, have the highest levels. When fertilisers wash into lakes, they cause an excessive growth of algae, an algal bloom. When the algae die, decomposers use up dissolved oxygen in breaking them down, and fish may die; this is eutrophication. Removing a top predator can let prey populations explode and overgraze plants, affecting many levels. Biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable, because many species can fill similar roles if one declines.
definitions: Living organisms interacting with each other and their physical environment.
A step in a food chain.
Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next.
Increase in concentration of a harmful chemical at higher trophic levels.
Over-enrichment of water with nutrients causing algal blooms and oxygen loss.

Food chains link to form food webs; each step is a trophic level.
About 10% of energy passes to the next level, so chains are short.
Biological magnification and eutrophication show how human activity disrupts ecosystems.

lessons.title: Managing Natural Resources
objectives: Explain the need to manage natural resources sustainably
Describe the conservation of forests and wildlife with stakeholders
Explain water harvesting and the problems of large dams
Discuss sustainable use of coal and petroleum
lessons.intro: Forests, water, wildlife, coal and petroleum are natural resources on which our lives and economy depend. Many are being used faster than they can be replaced, and their benefits are not always shared fairly. Managing natural resources means using them in a way that meets present needs, distributes benefits equitably and keeps them available for future generations. The three Rs, reduce, reuse and recycle, are a start, but larger choices about forests, water and energy also matter.
sections: Forests and wildlife

Forests are 'biodiversity hotspots' and provide timber, fuel, fodder, medicines, clean air and water. Different stakeholders have different interests: local people who depend on forests for daily needs, the Forest Department, industries that use forest products, and wildlife and nature enthusiasts. Successful conservation involves local communities. The Chipko movement in the Garhwal Himalayas in the 1970s, in which villagers hugged trees to stop felling, showed the power of local action. In West Bengal's Arabari forest, involving villagers in protecting sal forests led to their recovery. The Bishnoi community of Rajasthan has protected trees and animals for centuries; Amrita Devi Bishnoi gave her life in 1731 to save khejri trees.
Water for all

Rain falls unevenly, and much is lost as run-off. Traditional water-harvesting systems capture rainwater where it falls: khadins and kundis in Rajasthan, bandharas in Maharashtra, kulhs in Himachal Pradesh, and ponds and tanks in many states. Storing water underground through recharge has advantages: it does not evaporate, does not breed mosquitoes and is protected from contamination. Large dams provide irrigation, drinking water and electricity, but they can displace large numbers of people without adequate compensation, cost huge sums, and cause deforestation and loss of biodiversity; the debates over the Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada show these issues.
Coal and petroleum

Coal and petroleum formed from the remains of living things over millions of years and cannot be replaced once used. Burning them releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas causing global warming, as well as oxides of sulphur and nitrogen that cause acid rain and breathing problems. Using them sustainably means using them efficiently and reducing dependence on them: switching off lights and fans when not needed, using public transport, cycling or walking for short trips, using energy-efficient appliances and shifting to renewable sources such as solar and wind energy. Sustainable management balances development with the long-term health of the environment.
definitions: Using resources so they meet present needs and remain available for the future.
A person or group with an interest in a resource.
Collecting and storing rainwater for later use.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas formed from ancient living matter.
A 1970s movement in which villagers hugged trees to prevent felling.
examples: Rooftop rainwater harvesting is compulsory for new buildings in several Indian cities.
The Ganga Action Plan was launched in 1985 to reduce pollution in the river.

worked.answer: Communities who benefit from and understand the forest become protectors rather than opponents, making conservation lasting.

topics.title: Chemical Reactions and Acids, Bases and Salts
topics.description: Writing and balancing equations, types of reactions, and the chemistry of acids, bases and salts.

lessons.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
objectives: Identify signs of a chemical reaction
Write and balance chemical equations
Classify reactions: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox
Explain corrosion and rancidity
lessons.intro: When milk turns sour, iron rusts or food is digested, new substances are formed. These are chemical reactions. We recognise them by changes such as a change in state or colour, the release of a gas, or a change in temperature. Chemists describe reactions using chemical equations, which show reactants turning into products, with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides because mass is conserved.
sections: Writing and balancing equations

A word equation names the reactants and products: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. A chemical equation uses formulae: Mg + O₂ → MgO. This is unbalanced because there are two oxygen atoms on the left and one on the right. Balancing means adjusting the coefficients (numbers in front of formulae), never the subscripts: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Now there are two Mg and two O atoms on each side. States can be shown with (s), (l), (g) and (aq), and conditions such as heat or a catalyst can be written above the arrow. Balanced equations obey the law of conservation of mass.
Types of reactions

In a combination reaction, two or more substances form one product: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, which also releases heat (exothermic). In a decomposition reaction, one substance breaks into two or more: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating (thermal decomposition); silver chloride decomposes in sunlight (photolysis); water decomposes by electricity (electrolysis). In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. In a double displacement reaction, ions are exchanged, often forming a precipitate: Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄↓ + 2NaCl. Reactions that release heat are exothermic, such as respiration; those that absorb heat are endothermic.
Oxidation, reduction and everyday effects

Oxidation is the gain of oxygen (or loss of hydrogen) by a substance; reduction is the loss of oxygen (or gain of hydrogen). Both happen together in redox reactions: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, where copper oxide is reduced and hydrogen is oxidised. Corrosion is the slow attack of metals by air, moisture or acids: iron rusts, silver turns black and copper develops a green coating. It is prevented by painting, oiling and galvanising. Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils in food, giving a bad taste and smell; it is slowed by adding antioxidants, storing in airtight containers or flushing packets with nitrogen, as in chip packets.
definitions: A symbolic representation of a reaction using formulae.
An equation with equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides.
A reaction in which one substance breaks into simpler substances.
Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen.
Oxidation of fats and oils causing unpleasant taste and smell.
examples: Chip packets are filled with nitrogen to prevent rancidity.

Balance by changing coefficients, never subscripts.
Main types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and redox.
Corrosion and rancidity are everyday oxidation reactions that can be prevented.

lessons.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
objectives: Describe the chemical properties of acids and bases
Use the pH scale and indicators
Explain the importance of pH in everyday life
Describe the preparation and uses of common salts
lessons.intro: Acids and bases are among the most important groups of chemicals. In earlier grades you learnt that acids are sour and turn blue litmus red, while bases are bitter and turn red litmus blue. Now we look more closely at how they react, how their strength is measured using the pH scale, and how important salts such as baking soda, washing soda, bleaching powder and plaster of Paris are made and used.
sections: Reactions of acids and bases

Acids react with many metals to give a salt and hydrogen gas: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Acids react with metal carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky. Acids and bases neutralise each other: acid + base → salt + water, as in HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Metal oxides are basic and react with acids; non-metal oxides are acidic and react with bases. In water, acids produce hydrogen ions, H⁺ (present as H₃O⁺), and bases soluble in water, called alkalis, produce hydroxide ions, OH⁻. Mixing concentrated acid with water releases a lot of heat, so acid must always be added slowly to water, never water to acid.
The pH scale

The strength of acids and bases is measured on the pH scale from 0 to 14. A pH of 7 is neutral (pure water). Values below 7 are acidic, and the lower the number, the stronger the acid; values above 7 are basic, and the higher, the stronger the base. A universal indicator shows different colours at different pH values. pH matters in daily life: our body works within a narrow pH range; tooth decay starts when the mouth's pH falls below about 5.5, which is why basic toothpaste helps; indigestion from excess stomach acid is treated with antacids; plants need soil of suitable pH; and acid rain with pH below 5.6 harms rivers and aquatic life.
Important salts

Common salt, sodium chloride, is the raw material for many chemicals. Electrolysis of brine (the chlor-alkali process) gives sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen. Chlorine reacts with dry slaked lime to give bleaching powder, used for disinfecting water and bleaching cloth. Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃) releases carbon dioxide on heating, making cakes rise, and is used in antacids. Washing soda (sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) removes permanent hardness of water and is used in cleaning. Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O), made by heating gypsum, sets into a hard mass with water and is used for plastering fractured bones and making casts.
definitions: A scale from 0 to 14 measuring how acidic or basic a solution is.
A base that dissolves in water.
A mixture of indicators showing different colours at different pH values.
Electrolysis of brine producing NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.
Calcium sulphate hemihydrate, which sets hard when mixed with water.
examples: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2; soap solution about 10.
Baking powder contains baking soda and a mild acid such as tartaric acid.

worked.problem: Solutions A, B and C have pH 3, 7 and 11. Identify each and say which turns red litmus blue.
steps: pH 3 < 7: A is acidic.
pH 7: B is neutral.
pH 11 > 7: C is basic, so it turns red litmus blue.
worked.answer: A acidic, B neutral, C basic; C turns red litmus blue.

lessons.real_world: Soil testing guides farmers on adding lime or organic matter, toothpaste fights tooth decay by neutralising mouth acids, bleaching powder keeps drinking water safe, and plaster of Paris is used in hospitals for fractures and by artists for sculptures.
takeaways: Acids react with metals (giving H₂), carbonates (giving CO₂) and bases (neutralisation).
pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic; lower pH means stronger acid.
pH is vital in digestion, teeth, soil and the environment.
Common salt gives NaOH, Cl₂, bleaching powder, baking soda and washing soda; gypsum gives plaster of Paris.

topics.title: Electricity
topics.description: Electric current, potential difference, Ohm's law, resistance and circuits.

lessons.title: Electric Current and Ohm's Law
objectives: Define electric current, charge and potential difference
State Ohm's law and use V = IR
Explain factors affecting resistance and resistivity
Calculate electrical power and energy
lessons.intro: Switch on a fan and it starts turning; switch on a bulb and it glows. Electricity powers almost everything in modern life. But what actually flows in a wire, what pushes it, and why do some materials let it pass easily while others do not? In this lesson we define current, potential difference and resistance, and connect them through one of the most useful laws in physics: Ohm's law.
sections: Current and potential difference

Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge: I = Q ÷ t. Its SI unit is the ampere (A); one ampere is one coulomb of charge flowing per second. In metal wires, the moving charges are electrons. By convention, current is taken to flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, opposite to electron flow. Charges flow only when there is a potential difference (voltage) between two points, provided for example by a cell or battery. Potential difference is the work done to move a unit charge between two points: V = W ÷ Q, measured in volts (V). An ammeter, connected in series, measures current; a voltmeter, connected in parallel, measures potential difference.
Ohm's law and resistance

Georg Simon Ohm found that the current through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided its temperature remains constant: V ∝ I, or V = IR. The constant R is the resistance of the conductor, measured in ohms (Ω). Resistance is the property of a conductor that opposes the flow of current. A graph of V against I for such a conductor is a straight line through the origin. If a 12 V battery drives a current of 2 A through a resistor, R = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 Ω.
Factors affecting resistance, power and energy

Resistance increases with the length of the conductor and decreases with its area of cross-section: R = ρL/A, where ρ (rho) is the resistivity, a property of the material. Metals such as copper and aluminium have low resistivity and make good conductors; alloys such as nichrome have high resistivity and are used in heaters; glass and rubber are insulators. Resistance of most metals also increases with temperature. Electric power, the rate of using electrical energy, is P = VI = I²R = V²/R, measured in watts (W). Energy consumed is power × time; electricity bills use kilowatt-hours (kWh), called 'units': 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
definitions: The rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.
Work done per unit charge between two points, measured in volts.
V = IR at constant temperature for a metallic conductor.
A property of a material that determines its resistance for given dimensions.
The commercial unit of electrical energy, 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
examples: A 100 W bulb used for 10 hours consumes 1 kWh (one unit).
Heating elements are made of nichrome because of its high resistivity and high melting point.

lessons.title: Resistors in Series and Parallel and the Heating Effect
objectives: Calculate equivalent resistance in series and parallel
Explain current and voltage distribution in each arrangement
Explain why household circuits use parallel connections
Explain the heating effect of current and its applications
lessons.intro: In decorative light strings, if one bulb fails, sometimes all the lights go out, and sometimes only one does. The difference lies in how the bulbs are connected: in series or in parallel. The way resistors are combined changes the total resistance, the current and the voltage in a circuit. These ideas explain how our homes are wired safely and how heaters, irons and fuses work.
sections: Series combination

When resistors are connected end to end, they are in series. The same current flows through each, and the total potential difference is shared: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃. The equivalent resistance is the sum: Rₛ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃, so it is greater than any single resistance. For 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω in series across 10 V, Rₛ = 10 Ω, the current is 1 A, and the voltages are 2 V, 3 V and 5 V. In series, if one component breaks, the whole circuit is broken and all components stop working.
Parallel combination

When resistors are connected between the same two points, they are in parallel. Each has the same potential difference across it, and the total current is divided among them: I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃. The equivalent resistance is found from 1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃, so it is less than the smallest individual resistance. For 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel, 1/Rₚ = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so Rₚ = 2 Ω. Household appliances are connected in parallel so that each receives the full mains voltage (about 220 V in India), each can be switched on or off independently, and a fault in one does not stop the others.
Heating effect of current

When current flows through a resistor, electrical energy is converted into heat. Joule's law of heating states that the heat produced is H = I²Rt. The heat increases with the square of the current, with resistance and with time. This effect is used in electric irons, toasters, heaters, kettles and filament bulbs, where tungsten, with its very high melting point, glows white-hot. A fuse is a safety device: a short wire of low melting point connected in series with the circuit, which melts and breaks the circuit when excessive current flows due to a short circuit or overloading. Modern homes also use miniature circuit breakers (MCBs).
definitions: Resistors connected end to end so the same current flows through each.
Resistors connected across the same two points so each has the same voltage.
The single resistance that would have the same effect as a combination.
A safety wire that melts and breaks the circuit when current is too large.
examples: Two 4 Ω resistors in series give 8 Ω; in parallel they give 2 Ω.
A 10 A fuse protects a circuit by melting if the current exceeds 10 A.

lessons.real_world: House wiring uses parallel circuits so each appliance works independently at full voltage, and fuses or MCBs protect against fires from overloading. Electric kettles, irons and immersion rods are practical uses of the heating effect.

Parallel: 1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …; same voltage, current divides.
Homes use parallel wiring for independent operation at full voltage.
Heat H = I²Rt; fuses use this effect to protect circuits.
